decks.title: Reproductive Health — Part 1: Programmes, population and contraception
goals: Define reproductive health and describe India’s programmes
Explain population explosion and the government’s role
Describe natural, barrier, IUD, hormonal and surgical methods of contraception and their modes of action

slides.heading: Reproductive Health
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a healthy society needs people who are healthy in every aspect of reproduction.

visual.alt: Flow showing four aspects that make up reproductive health

slides.narration: According to the World Health Organisation, reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A society with people who have physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal interactions is reproductively healthy.

slides.heading: Programmes in India
slides.body_md: India was among the first countries to start national programmes for reproductive health.

rows: Audio-visual and print media; sex education in schools to give correct information and discourage myths
Medical help for problems such as pregnancy, delivery, STDs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility
Ban on amniocentesis for sex determination to check female foeticide; mass immunisation

visual.alt: Table of reproductive health programmes and actions in India

slides.narration: These programmes aim to create awareness, provide medical help and build a reproductively healthy society. Research and better health care have led to lower maternal and infant mortality, more medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care.

slides.heading: Population explosion
slides.body_md: India’s population was about **350 million** at independence, reached **1 billion** by 2000 and **1.2 billion** in 2011. Rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR), and an increase in people of reproducible age, caused this rise.

slides.narration: A population that grows at a steady rate keeps doubling in fixed periods of time. At about two percent a year, numbers double roughly every thirty-five years. Such growth strains food, housing, water and other basic needs.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: doubling time
slides.body_md: A population of 100 grows at 2 percent a year. In about how many years will it double, and what will it be after 105 years?
bullets: Doubling time $= \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.02} \approx 35.0$, about **35 years**.
105 years is about three doublings: $100 \times 2^3 = 800$ (exactly $100 \times 1.02^{105} \approx 800$).

visual.alt: Worked table: doubling about every 35 years

slides.narration: At two percent a year, the population doubles about every thirty-five years. In one hundred and five years it doubles three times, so one hundred becomes about eight hundred. Small yearly rates make very large numbers over a lifetime.

slides.heading: The government’s role
slides.body_md: The government encourages smaller families through motivation and law.

rows: Motivating smaller families by using contraceptive methods
“Hum Do Hamare Do” (we two, our two); many young couples now adopt a one-child norm
Raised to 18 years for females and 21 years for males
Given to couples with small families

visual.alt: Table of government measures against population explosion

slides.narration: Raising the legal marriageable age delays the start of families, and incentives reward couples who keep their families small. The most important tool, however, is contraception.

slides.heading: Natural and barrier methods
slides.body_md: An ideal contraceptive is user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible, with no or least side-effects, and does not interfere with sexual drive or the sexual act.

rows: Avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the cycle, when ovulation is expected
Male withdraws before ejaculation, avoiding insemination
No ovulation while the mother breast-feeds fully, up to about six months after parturition
Barrier: prevent sperms from meeting the ovum; also protect against STDs
Rubber barriers that cover the cervix; reusable; spermicidal creams and jellies increase effectiveness

visual.alt: Table of natural and barrier methods with modes of action

slides.narration: Natural methods avoid meeting of the ovum and sperm and have no side-effects, but their failure rate is high. Condoms are popular because they also protect the user from sexually transmitted diseases.

slides.heading: The fertile period
slides.body_md: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation is expected around **day 14**. The chances of fertilisation are high from **day 10 to day 17**, so couples avoiding conception abstain during this period.

slides.narration: Periodic abstinence depends on knowing when ovulation is likely. Because cycles vary, the method is not very reliable, but it costs nothing and has no side-effects.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a longer cycle
slides.body_md: A woman’s cycles are regularly 30 days long. Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period. Which days form her fertile period, using the same rule as days 10–17 of a 28-day cycle?
bullets: Ovulation $= 30 - 14 = $ day 16.
Fertile period: day 16 $- 4 =$ **day 12** to day 16 $+ 3 =$ **day 19**.

visual.alt: Worked table: fertile period days 12–19

slides.narration: The time after ovulation is fairly constant at about fourteen days, so in a thirty-day cycle ovulation is near day sixteen. Counting four days before and three after gives days twelve to nineteen.

slides.body_md: **IUDs** are inserted by doctors or trained nurses into the uterus through the vagina. Types: **non-medicated** (Lippes loop), **copper-releasing** (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and **hormone-releasing** (Progestasert, LNG-20).

slides.narration: IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus. Copper ions released suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms. They are ideal for women who want to delay pregnancy or space children.

slides.heading: Hormonal methods
slides.body_md: Small doses of **progestogens** or **progestogen–estrogen** combinations are used by females as **pills**, **injections** or **implants** under the skin.

rows: Taken daily for 21 days, starting within the first five days of the cycle; after a gap of 7 days, repeated. They inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus to retard sperms
A once-a-week, non-steroidal pill developed by CDRI, Lucknow
Same mode of action; effective for much longer
Progestogens, combinations or an IUD within 72 hours of unprotected coitus

visual.alt: Table of hormonal methods with their action

slides.narration: Hormonal pills are very effective with fewer side-effects. They work by stopping ovulation and implantation and by making cervical mucus hostile to sperms. Emergency methods within seventy-two hours can be used after rape or unprotected intercourse.

slides.heading: Surgical methods
slides.body_md: **Sterilisation** is a terminal method for those who want no more children. **Vasectomy**: a small part of the **vas deferens** is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum. **Tubectomy**: a small part of the **fallopian tube** is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina.

slides.heading: MTP, infertility and STDs
slides.body_md: Part 2 — safe practices and medical help in reproduction.

visual.alt: Flow of the four topics of this part

slides.narration: This part looks at four areas of reproductive health care: terminating unwanted pregnancies safely, detecting genetic disorders before birth, helping couples who cannot conceive, and preventing infections passed on through sexual contact.

slides.heading: Medical termination of pregnancy
slides.body_md: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is **MTP** (induced abortion). India legalised MTP in **1971**, with strict conditions to prevent misuse such as **female foeticide**.

rows: Getting rid of unwanted pregnancies due to casual unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure; or when continuing the pregnancy could harm the mother or the foetus
Considered relatively safe during the first trimester
Performed by registered medical practitioners within the time limits and conditions of the law
Misuse for sex-selective abortion of normal female foetuses, and unsafe procedures by unqualified people

visual.alt: Table of the purposes, safety, conditions and concerns of MTP

slides.narration: MTP plays a role in reducing unwanted pregnancies, but it is not a method of contraception. It must be done by qualified doctors within the law. Illegal abortions by unqualified people are unsafe and can be fatal.

slides.heading: Amniocentesis
slides.body_md: **Amniocentesis** is a foetal sex-determination and disorder test based on the chromosomal pattern in the **amniotic fluid** surrounding the developing embryo. Foetal cells in the fluid are cultured and their chromosomes analysed.

slides.heading: Infertility
slides.body_md: A large number of couples are **infertile**: they cannot produce children despite unprotected sexual cohabitation. The reasons may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological, and the problem may lie in **either partner**.

rows: Male or female partner; in India the woman is often wrongly blamed
Specialised health-care units (infertility clinics) diagnose and treat many disorders
Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) can help couples have children

visual.alt: Table of key points about infertility

slides.narration: Infertility is not always the woman’s fault; it can just as often lie with the man. Many cases can be diagnosed and treated, and where they cannot, assisted reproductive technologies offer another way to have children.

slides.heading: Assisted reproductive technologies
slides.body_md: ART are special techniques that help infertile couples. (The ISC syllabus needs their definitions and applications.)

rows: Fertilisation outside the body in almost similar conditions, followed by embryo transfer
Zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) transferred into the fallopian tube
Embryo with more than 8 blastomeres transferred into the uterus
Ovum from a donor transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment
Sperm directly injected into the ovum in the laboratory
Semen from the husband or a donor introduced into the vagina or uterus when the male cannot inseminate or has a low sperm count

visual.alt: Table of assisted reproductive technologies

slides.narration: Each technique bypasses a particular problem. If the oviducts are blocked, fertilisation can happen in the laboratory. If sperms are few, they can be injected directly into the ovum. Adoption is another option for childless couples.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: matching the technique
slides.body_md: Suggest a suitable technique for each case.
bullets: An embryo of 6 blastomeres is ready for transfer → **ZIFT** (into the fallopian tube).
An embryo of 16 blastomeres is ready for transfer → **IUT** (into the uterus).
A woman cannot produce ova but can sustain a pregnancy → **GIFT** with a donor ovum.
A man has a very low sperm count → **IUI** (artificial insemination) or **ICSI**.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four cases to techniques

slides.narration: Match the technique to the problem. Early embryos of up to eight cells go into the fallopian tube, by ZIFT, while larger embryos go into the uterus, by IUT. A woman without ova can receive a donor ovum by GIFT, and a low sperm count can be overcome by IUI or ICSI.

slides.body_md: In which technique is a sperm injected directly into an ovum?

slides.heading: Sexually transmitted diseases
slides.body_md: Diseases or infections transmitted through **sexual intercourse** are STDs (also called venereal diseases or reproductive tract infections).

visual.alt: Table of eight STDs and their causes

slides.narration: Some of these infections, such as hepatitis B and HIV, also spread by sharing injection needles and surgical instruments with infected persons, by transfusion of infected blood, or from an infected mother to her foetus. Except for hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV infections, the others are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

slides.heading: Symptoms, complications and prevention
slides.body_md: Early symptoms are often **minor**: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region. Infected females may often be **asymptomatic**, so the infection may go undetected.

rows: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility, even cancer of the reproductive tract
Persons in the age group 15–24 years
Avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always use condoms during coitus; consult a qualified doctor early in case of doubt

visual.alt: Table of complications and prevention of STDs

slides.narration: Because early symptoms are mild and the social stigma attached to these diseases deters people from seeking help, many cases are diagnosed late. Simple precautions and early treatment prevent serious complications.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spread and prevention
slides.body_md: A clinic sees three patients. Name the likely infection or risk and the key advice.
bullets: A patient with hepatitis B who never had sexual contact but shared injection needles → infection by **sharing needles**; advise using **sterile, disposable needles**.
A pregnant woman with HIV → risk of **transmission to the foetus**; she needs medical care during pregnancy and delivery.
A young person with genital discharge and itching → possible **gonorrhoea, chlamydiasis or trichomoniasis**; advise **early consultation** and **condom use**.

visual.alt: Worked table of three patients with routes and advice

slides.narration: Not every sexually transmitted infection spreads only through sex. Hepatitis B and HIV can also spread by needles, transfusion or from mother to foetus. In every case, early diagnosis and simple precautions make a big difference.

slides.heading: Quick check: STDs
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about STDs in females.
slides.narration: Quick check. Are early symptoms always noticeable?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: MTP legal since 1971 under strict conditions; relatively safe in the first trimester; misuse for female foeticide is illegal.
Amniocentesis detects chromosomal disorders; its use for sex determination is banned.
Infertility can lie with either partner; ART: IVF, ZIFT (up to 8 blastomeres), IUT (more than 8), GIFT, ICSI, AI/IUI.
STDs: gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, trichomoniasis, genital herpes, genital warts, hepatitis B, AIDS; hepatitis B, herpes and HIV not completely curable.
Complications: PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, cancer; prevention by safe practices and early consultation.

visual.alt: Summary table of transfer sites in ART

slides.narration: To recap: MTP and amniocentesis are legal medical tools with strict limits. Infertility can affect either partner and can often be helped by assisted reproductive technologies. And sexually transmitted diseases are preventable by safe practices and early treatment.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Expand **MTP, ZIFT, GIFT, IUT, ICSI, IUI** correctly.
Give the **causative organism** of each STD.
Name STDs that are **not completely curable**.
State why amniocentesis for sex determination is **banned**.

sections.heading: 1. Reproductive health, programmes and population
sections.body_md:
**Reproductive health** (WHO): a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction — **physical, emotional, behavioural and social**. A reproductively healthy society has people with physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects.

**Programmes.** India initiated **family planning** in **1951**; improved programmes now cover wider areas under **Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH)**. Actions include: creating awareness through audio-visual and print media; **sex education** in schools to provide right information and discourage myths and misconceptions; educating people about birth control, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care, breast-feeding, equal opportunities for male and female children; medical facilities for pregnancy, delivery, STDs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility; the statutory **ban on amniocentesis for sex determination** to check female foeticide; and **mass child immunisation**. Better care has reduced **maternal and infant mortality** and increased medically assisted deliveries.

**Population explosion.** India’s population was about **350 million** at independence, close to **1 billion** in 2000 and about **1.2 billion** in 2011. Causes: rapid decline in the **death rate**, **maternal mortality rate (MMR)** and **infant mortality rate (IMR)**, and an increase in the number of people in the reproducible age. The growth rate in 2011 was below 2 percent (about 20 per 1000 per year), which still increases the population quickly. Consequences: scarcity of basic requirements such as food, shelter and clothing.

**Government measures:** motivating smaller families through contraception (slogan **“Hum Do Hamare Do”**; many couples adopt a one-child norm); raising the **marriageable age** to **18 years for females** and **21 years for males**; **incentives** to couples with small families.

sections.heading: 2. Methods of contraception
sections.body_md:
An **ideal contraceptive** is user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no or least side-effects, and does not interfere with sexual drive, desire or the sexual act.

**Natural methods** (avoid chances of ovum and sperm meeting):
- **Periodic abstinence:** avoid coitus from **day 10 to 17** of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected.
- **Withdrawal (coitus interruptus):** the male withdraws before ejaculation, avoiding insemination.
- **Lactational amenorrhea:** absence of menstruation and ovulation during intense lactation after parturition; effective only up to about **six months**.
These have no side-effects but high failure rates.

**Barrier methods** (prevent ovum and sperm from meeting): **condoms** (male and female; disposable; also protect against **STDs and AIDS**); **diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults** (rubber barriers inserted to cover the cervix; reusable). **Spermicidal** creams, jellies and foams are used with them to increase efficiency.

**Intrauterine devices (IUDs)**, inserted by doctors or trained nurses into the uterus through the vagina:
- **Non-medicated:** Lippes loop.
- **Copper-releasing:** CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 — **copper ions** suppress **sperm motility** and fertilising capacity.
- **Hormone-releasing:** Progestasert, LNG-20 — make the uterus **unsuitable for implantation** and the cervix **hostile to sperms**.
IUDs increase **phagocytosis** of sperms within the uterus. They are ideal for females who want to **delay pregnancy** or **space children**; one of the most widely accepted methods in India.

**Hormonal methods** (pills, injections, implants of **progestogens** or **progestogen–estrogen** combinations): pills are taken daily for **21 days** starting within the first five days of the cycle, then after a gap of **7 days** repeated. They **inhibit ovulation and implantation** and alter the quality of **cervical mucus** to prevent or retard entry of sperms. **Saheli**, a new oral contraceptive for females, is a once-a-week, **non-steroidal** pill developed at the **Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow**. Injections and implants under the skin act in the same way but over a much longer period. Progestogens, combinations or IUDs used **within 72 hours** of coitus are effective as **emergency contraceptives**.

**Surgical methods (sterilisation)** — terminal methods that block gamete transport: **vasectomy** (a small part of the **vas deferens** removed or tied through a small incision on the scrotum) and **tubectomy** (a small part of the **fallopian tube** removed or tied through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina). Highly effective, but reversibility is very poor.

Possible side-effects of improper use include nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding and even breast cancer, though these are not very significant.

sections.heading: 3. MTP and amniocentesis
sections.body_md:
**Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)** is the intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term (induced abortion). Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year all over the world. The Government of India legalised MTP in **1971**, with strict conditions to avoid its misuse, such as indiscriminate and illegal **female foeticide**, which is reported to be high in India.
- **Reasons:** to get rid of unwanted pregnancies due to casual unprotected intercourse or failure of contraception during coitus or rapes; and in cases where continuing the pregnancy could be **harmful or even fatal** to the mother or the foetus.
- MTPs are considered relatively **safe during the first trimester**. They must be performed by **registered medical practitioners** within the **time limits and conditions** laid down by law; MTP by unqualified quacks is unsafe and can be fatal. MTP is not a contraceptive.

**Amniocentesis** is a foetal sex-determination test based on the chromosomal pattern in the **amniotic fluid** surrounding the developing embryo. It can detect **genetic and chromosomal disorders** (for example Down’s syndrome) in the foetus, but its misuse to find the sex of the foetus led to female foeticide; its use for **sex determination is banned** by law in India.

A test of foetal cells in amniotic fluid for chromosomal disorders.
Abortion of a female foetus because of its sex; illegal in India.

sections.heading: 4. Infertility and assisted reproductive technologies
sections.body_md:
A large number of couples all over the world, including India, are **infertile**: unable to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual cohabitation. The reasons could be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological. In India the female is often blamed, but the problem is quite often in the **male partner**. Specialised health-care units (**infertility clinics**) help in diagnosis and corrective treatment, and where correction is not possible, **assisted reproductive technologies (ART)** help.

- **In vitro fertilisation (IVF)** — fertilisation outside the body in almost similar conditions as in the body, followed by **embryo transfer (ET)**: popularly the **test-tube baby** programme. Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and induced to form a zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory.
- **ZIFT (zygote intra-fallopian transfer):** the zygote or early embryo (**up to 8 blastomeres**) is transferred into the **fallopian tube**.
- **IUT (intra-uterine transfer):** an embryo with **more than 8 blastomeres** is transferred into the **uterus**.
- **GIFT (gamete intra-fallopian transfer):** transfer of an **ovum from a donor** into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development.
- **ICSI (intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection):** a sperm is directly injected into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory.
- **AI (artificial insemination) / IUI (intra-uterine insemination):** semen from the husband or a healthy donor is introduced into the vagina or into the uterus — useful when the male cannot inseminate or has a **very low sperm count**.
Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation (in the female) can also be transferred for further development.

ART needs high precision, specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so it is available only in a few centres; emotional, religious and social factors are also deterrents. **Legal adoption** is one of the best methods for couples looking for parenthood.

sections.heading: 5. Sexually transmitted diseases
sections.body_md:
Diseases or infections transmitted through **sexual intercourse** are **sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)**, also called venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI).

| Disease | Causative agent |
|---|---|
| Gonorrhoea | *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (bacterium) |
| Syphilis | *Treponema pallidum* (bacterium) |
| Chlamydiasis | *Chlamydia trachomatis* (bacterium) |
| Trichomoniasis | *Trichomonas vaginalis* (protozoan) |
| Genital herpes | Herpes simplex virus |
| Genital warts | Human papillomavirus |
| Hepatitis B | Hepatitis B virus |
| AIDS | Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) |

**Transmission:** mainly sexual; **hepatitis B and HIV** also by sharing injection needles and surgical instruments, transfusion of infected blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus.

**Curability:** except for **hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV** infections, the others are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

**Symptoms:** early symptoms are minor — **itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings** in the genital region. Infected females may often be **asymptomatic**, so they may remain undetected for long; the social stigma attached also deters people from timely detection and treatment.

**Complications:** pelvic inflammatory diseases (**PID**), abortions, still births, **ectopic pregnancies**, **infertility** or even **cancer of the reproductive tract**. People in the **15–24 years** age group are most at risk.

**Prevention:** avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always try to use **condoms** during coitus; in case of doubt, go to a **qualified doctor** for early detection and complete treatment.

Pelvic inflammatory disease, a complication of untreated STDs.
Implantation of the embryo outside the uterus, such as in the fallopian tube.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling MTP a method of contraception.
- Mixing ZIFT (up to 8 blastomeres, fallopian tube) and IUT (more than 8, uterus).
- Writing GIFT as transfer of an embryo (it is transfer of a donor ovum).
- Saying copper IUDs act by inhibiting ovulation (they suppress sperm motility; pills inhibit ovulation).
- Listing syphilis as incurable (hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV are not completely curable).
- Blaming only the female partner for infertility.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: expansions (MTP, ZIFT, GIFT, IUT, ICSI, IUI), pathogens, examples of IUDs, a reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: modes of action of contraceptives; ART matching; STD symptoms and prevention; MTP conditions.
- 5-mark questions in parts: contraception methods; population and government measures; infertility and ART; STDs.
